articles.title: Trump faces backlash over plans to import Russian diesel ahead of US midterms
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is facing bipartisan criticism over his decision to allow Russian diesel into the US market, as rising fuel prices linked to the
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is facing bipartisan criticism over his decision to allow Russian diesel into the US market, as rising fuel prices linked to the Iran war threaten to become a political liability for his Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections.Trump announced on Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by additional shipments in the coming months, to help ease global fuel shortages and bring down prices for American consumers.The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, who argue that easing restrictions on Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with funds to continue its war against Ukraine.The backlash comes just weeks after Trump signed legislation authorising fresh sanctions and tariffs against countries importing Russian oil and gas.A bipartisan group of seven senators on Sunday urged the president to reverse course, saying the US should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russian forces continue to kill Ukrainian civilians.“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement.The group included Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, along with Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.The US Treasury Department is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7 to facilitate the shipments, according to reports. Other Russian assets, including those held in American banks, remain frozen.What is in the Russia diesel deal?Trump said Russia would release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another one million tonnes thereafter.He also referred to a further three million tonnes to be delivered within a short period, depending on the condition of Russian refineries damaged in Ukrainian attacks.Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the figures to state-owned news agency Tass, adding that exports could eventually reach three million tonnes per month.“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the arrangement in an interview with Fox News, saying it would operate through existing legal channels available to the administration to help bring down prices. He rejected claims that the agreement would violate US law.Some Republicans have also backed Trump's approach. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer described it as an example of the president thinking outside the box to address the financial pressure on Americans.Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso said the sanctions legislation gave Trump flexibility and additional leverage in dealing with Putin.However, other Republicans have called for tougher action against Moscow. Senator Lisa Murkowski urged Trump to use the new law to increase pressure on Russia rather than allow it to earn additional revenue from diesel exports. Republican Representative Don Bacon also argued that buying Russian fuel was the wrong way to bring down prices.Democrats have been more sharply critical. Representative Steny Hoyer called the deal outrageous, while Representative Bill Keating described it as a disturbing capitulation to Putin. Senator Chris Van Hollen accused Trump of seeking to finance Russia's war against Ukraine after the Iran conflict drove up fuel prices.Fuel prices add to Trump's midterm challengeThe dispute comes at a politically sensitive time for Trump, with next month's midterm elections set to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress.The US-Israel war with Iran, which began at the end of February, has disrupted crude oil supplies and pushed up global energy prices. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for American farmers, ranchers and truckers, who depend on the fuel to operate machinery and transport goods.The average price of diesel in the US stood at $6.28 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association, down from a record $6.53 at the end of September.The rising cost of fuel has added to public dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and the Iran war. Polls indicate that a majority of Americans disapprove of his performance on both issues, putting additional pressure on the administration to demonstrate that it can bring prices down before voters head to the polls.Analysts have questioned whether Russia can deliver the promised volumes and whether the shipments would significantly reduce costs for American consumers. The US consumes approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel per day, meaning the initial 300,000-tonne shipment would account for only a fraction of its daily demand.The deal has also drawn criticism from US allies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a gift to Putin, arguing that the arrangement would provide financial support to Russia while its war against Ukraine continues. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting have also criticised the move, calling for greater pressure on Moscow to end the conflict.Trump announces energy ceasefire between Russia and UkraineAmid the controversy, Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, without providing further details.The proposed arrangement would halt attacks on the two countries' energy infrastructure. Zelensky welcomed the announcement but said Kyiv was awaiting details and confirmation from Moscow.“The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky wrote on X. He added that Ukraine expected Putin to follow through on Trump's announcement.There was no immediate response from Moscow.The energy ceasefire could offer a potential opening for reducing attacks on critical infrastructure, but the diesel arrangement has exposed divisions in Washington over how to balance domestic economic pressures with the US policy of pressuring Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.With fuel prices weighing on voters ahead of the midterms, Trump faces the challenge of delivering relief to American consumers without further alienating lawmakers who believe his Russia policy risks undermining efforts to end the war.You use AI every day. articles.title: Robert E Hall, Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for macroeconomic stabilisation models
articles.summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford for their contributions to understanding macroeconomic
articles.body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford for their contributions to understanding macroeconomic stabilisation, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Monday. The two economists were recognised “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.”"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs," said the Academy in its press release.Robert E Hall earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of California, Berkeley, and a PhD in economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), while Michael Woodford holds a bachelor’s degree from the University of Chicago, a law degree from Yale Law School and a PhD in economics from MIT.They both were recognised for developing economic models that have helped governments and central banks better manage economic fluctuations. Their work showed how timely changes in interest rates, government spending and taxation could help reduce the impact of recessions and prevent economies from overheating.Their research helped address the limitations of earlier economic models, particularly those exposed during the oil crises of the 1970s, when high inflation, unemployment and weak growth occurred simultaneously. Instead of relying mainly on broad economic indicators such as inflation, production and consumption, the two economists developed models based on how individual households and businesses make financial decisions.A key finding of their work was that people and businesses make decisions based not only on current economic conditions but also on their expectations of the future. This showed how governments and central banks could influence economic activity by clearly communicating their policy plans. Their models have since become important tools for designing monetary and fiscal policies and responding to economic shocks.“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.Unlike the other Nobel Prizes, the Economics Prize was not established by Alfred Nobel in his will. It was instituted in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank, Sweden’s central bank, to mark its 300th anniversary, and was first awarded in 1969 to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen. Officially known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, it is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences under the same principles as the original Nobel Prizes. The prize money is funded by Sweden’s central bank and is equal to that awarded in the other Nobel categories. Meanwhile, two Indian-born economists have won the prize in this category. Amartya Sen won in 1998 for his contributions to welfare economics, and Abhijit Banerjee in 2019, who shared the award with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.You use AI every day. articles.title: Poland deploys 20,000 cops in schools, inspects 80k educational institutions amid rising youth violence
articles.summary: Around 20,000 police officers are being deployed to schools across Poland on Monday after Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged to tackle what he described
articles.body: Around 20,000 police officers are being deployed to schools across Poland on Monday after Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged to tackle what he described as growing violence among young people.The deployment aims to strengthen security at schools following three recent stabbings within four days, Reuters reported.On Monday, police said they had inspected around 80,000 educational institutions and detained 135 people since Friday.Tusk, who chaired a crisis meeting on Sunday, said the glorification of violence in certain corners of the internet was having a harmful impact on young people."We have observed a rise in the fascination with violence, both in Poland and worldwide... we are witnessing a grim trend of violence," Tusk said, adding that content promoting Nazi ideology and a "cult of strength", along with violent computer games, were major contributing factors.In one case, police said a boy had created a model of his school in the Roblox game and simulated attacks on students. He was found in possession of a firearm, ammunition and knives.However, authorities dismissed rumours that the violent incidents were connected to an online challenge or an organised group. Reuters reported.On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a caretaker and injured two teachers at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, north-east of Warsaw.On Wednesday, a 19-year-old injured 10 people, including himself, at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital.The most recent attack took place on Saturday, when three people were injured at a further education college in Warsaw. It was Poland's third stabbing attack at an educational institution in four days.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said a "clear message" was needed."There will be no tolerance for any attacks on Polish children, nor for the descent of public life into anarchy," Kierwinski told state news channel TVP Info.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to lose $245m as The Social Recknoning also struggles at box office
articles.summary: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.
articles.body:
Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.

Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.

It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".

The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.

That would put Digger in the same bracket as other films which lost upwards of $100m, including 1995's Cutthroat Island, 2002's The Adventures of Pluto Nash, 2005's Sahara and 2012's John Carter.

Other films estimated to have lost nine-figure sums include Mars Needs Moms (2011), Amsterdam (2022), The 13th Warrior (1999), The Marvels (2023) and Speed Racer (2008).

Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of major franchises starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of Top Gun and Mission: Impossible.

Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.

The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.

However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).

Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

The film is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.

Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself".

Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend.

The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation.

Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (£6.8m).

The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices.

The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast.

articles.title: Julie Hesmondhalgh exits Celebrity Traitors 'with head held high'

articles.body:
Actress Julie Hesmondhalgh - the most recently banished contestant from The Celebrity Traitors - says she left the show with her "head held high".

The former Coronation Street star, from Accrington in Lancashire, starred as a faithful contestant in the second series of the BBC One show - before being voted out by other players on Friday's episode.

She said she "had no idea" she was going to be banished, but it "became clear it was going to be me and I was a bit worried".

"I did feel it was my time," she told BBC Radio Manchester , adding: "I left with my head held high... but I had some very gratifying apologetic texts on Friday night."

The actress said being on the game show had been an "amazing experience".

"I've watched every episode of them all - even the New Zealand one."

articles.title: Daniel Kinahan's lawyers to apply for bail in due course, court hears
articles.summary: He is charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.
articles.body:
An application for bail is to be made on the behalf of Daniel Kinahan in due course, the Special Criminal Court has heard.

The application will be made through the High Court in Dublin.

Darragh Mackin of Phoenix Law, who is Kinahan's solicitor, appeared in court on Monday where he confirmed an application will be made for bail.

Kinahan is charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.

Mackin also told the court Kinahan's defence legal team is looking for an expert to examine the digital evidence and that they are seeking information on other international investigations that Kinahan was acquitted of.

The prosecuting barrister from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) said there is "complex factual matrix" behind Kinahan's single charge.

He told the court that behind Kinahan's extradition from Dubai earlier this year, a statement of facts which is 189 pages long was behind it.

Kinahan was remanded and scheduled to appear in person at court again on 21 December.

The DPP barrister said the book of evidence should be ready by that time.

This is Kinahan's third time before the special criminal court and second time he appeared in person.

He was dressed in a grey suit with a black shirt and black glasses.

Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April and extradited on 9 August when he was flown back to Ireland on board the Irish government's jet.

articles.title: Make sure use of AI is safe, Guernsey data watchdog warns
articles.summary: Guernsey's data protection authority is reminding businesses to use AI safely to protect clients.
articles.body:
Guernsey's data protection authority has warned the responsibility for protecting client data "can't be outsourced" amid concerns over the speed of artificial intelligence development.

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector called for a slow down and last month it was revealed a "rogue" OpenAI agent hacked Australia's online medical system .

Brent Homan, commissioner for the Office of the Data Protection Authority, said Guernsey businesses needed to reflect on their use of AI seriously.

"Ultimately any organisation can outsource certain responsibilities, but they can't outsource their accountability," he said.

Homan said while the bailiwick was yet to see a reported AI-directed breach, it was important Guernsey companies were careful about security.

"It's really important for organisations to ensure that they have good contracts in place and assure themselves of the security of the third parties that they use," he said.

Matt Palmer, the director Guernsey and Jersey's cyber security centres, said AI was here to stay "whether we like it or not".

He said his organisation was adapting to the potential cybersecurity risks presented by AI but he felt positive about the bailiwick's position.

Companies should make use of existing resources to ensure their use of AI was safe, he added.

Palmer said: "I don't think it's quite the sort of goblin of fear that sometimes it is made out to be.

"What we need is careful testing, good controls, sensible and pragmatic adoption, we can deal with a lot of these risks. It is never going to be risk-free."

articles.title: ‘Goddess of bombs’: Tanot Mata temple in Jaisalmer witnesses a massive Navratri turnout
articles.summary: JAISALMER: For generations of troops guarding India’s western frontier, Tanot Mata is more than a deity.
articles.body: JAISALMER: For generations of troops guarding India’s western frontier, Tanot Mata is more than a deity. Revered as the ‘Goddess of Bombs’, the presiding deity of the Tanot Mata Temple near the India-Pakistan border in Rajasthan’s Jaisalmer district holds a special place in the faith of security personnel, rooted in accounts of unexploded bombs during the 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan wars.The temple’s enduring association with these wartime accounts has made it a place of deep devotion for soldiers and civilians alike. Now, as Navratri begins, thousands of devotees are making their way to the shrine to seek the blessings of Tanot Mata.Located around 120km from Jaisalmer, the Tanot Mata Temple in Tanot village is popularly known as Bamo Wali Devi, or the ‘Goddess of Bombs’. Its religious significance remains closely intertwined with the military history of the border region and the faith of those who guard it.More than 20,000 devotees from across the country visited the 1,200-year-old temple on Sunday, the first day of the 10-day Navratri fair, which began with the traditional Ghatasthapana ceremony.According to popular accounts, hundreds of bombs fired by Pakistani forces during the 1965 and 1971 wars fell in the temple area but did not explode within its premises.The accounts strengthened the faith of local residents and security personnel in the deity. Following the 1965 war, Army and Border Security Force (BSF) personnel developed a special reverence for the temple and contributed to its development.The shrine has remained a symbol of faith for personnel posted in the border region. Devotees have also linked the temple’s protective legacy to Operation Sindoor, believing that Tanot Mata’s blessings were behind the failure of drones that reportedly crossed into Indian territory from Pakistan to cause damage in Jaisalmer. Such interpretations reflect the religious beliefs associated with the shrine.Traditional rituals mark Navratri openingThe 10-day fair began with the installation of the sacred Kalash amid drumbeats and traditional rituals. A grand procession was taken out to the temple, followed by a havan and yajna on the temple premises. BSF officers and personnel participated in the rituals and offered oblations.The ceremony was attended by Linzkai Sitalu, Commandant of the BSF’s 26th Battalion; Second-in-Command Madan Goyal; Deepankar Sharma; Deputy Commandants Anmol Bhagat and Sushil Kumar; and other BSF officers and personnel.Three aartis were performed on the opening day, and the same schedule will continue throughout Navratri. A community kitchen is serving prasad to devotees from morning till evening.BSF steps up arrangements for pilgrimsGiven the temple’s location in a sensitive border region and the large number of visitors expected during the festival, the BSF has strengthened arrangements for devotees’ darshan, food, medical assistance and other essential facilities.Under the guidance of the Inspector General of the BSF Rajasthan Frontier and the direction of Jitendra Singh Binji, Deputy Inspector General of the BSF’s North Sector, the 26th Battalion has made arrangements to facilitate the pilgrimage. A medical camp has been established, and police personnel have been deployed alongside BSF troops.The temple has been decorated and illuminated for Navratri. A large LCD screen has been installed outside the premises so that devotees can watch the deity’s darshan and aarti during periods of heavy crowding.BSF personnel also serve as priests and oversee the temple’s upkeep and arrangements for pilgrims. Officials said the shrine’s growing popularity was evident from the number of devotees undertaking the journey on foot. Temporary shops have also been set up around the temple to cater to visitors.Meanwhile, Ghatasthapana was also performed at Ghantiyali Mata Temple, where devotees participated in havan rituals. Arrangements at religious sites across the region are being strengthened to accommodate the growing number of visitors during Navratri.Stay updated with the latest Jodhpur news. articles.title: Barbara Hepworth dawn sculpture could fetch £8m at auction
articles.summary: A post-war sculpture inspired by the Cornish landscape is set to go under the hammer.
articles.body:
A "pivotal masterwork" by Dame Barbara Hepworth inspired by the Cornish landscape is expected to sell for up to £8m at auction.

Hepworth carved Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946 and named it after the Greek goddess of dawn.

Auction house Christie said it would be the highlight of a modern British and Irish art sale on 21 October and was estimated to sell between £5m and £8m.

The auction house holds the world auction record for a Hepworth piece, The Family of Man: Ancestor II, which sold for £10.7m in 2023.

Auctioneers said the Cornish landscape "strongly influenced" Hepworth, who was born in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, and moved to Cornwall in 1939.

She moved to St Ives with her artist husband Ben Nicholson and their family at the outbreak of World War Two.

She lived and worked in Trewyn Studio, which is now the Tate Barbara Hepworth Museum, from 1949 until her death in a fire in 1975.

Auctioneers said the Cornish light, sea, cliffs and ancient stones "became central to her artistic practice" and influenced her technique of adding colour to her sculptures.

Alice Murray, Christie's head of modern British and Irish art, said the sculpture was carved "the year the world began again" after the war.

"Three hollows, painted blue, grey and white, catch the light like the first minutes of morning," she said.

The auction house said the sculpture was a "pivotal" piece by Hepworth, who became a leading light in the Cornish artistic community .

It said the post-war work "suggests emergence, awakening and renewal: a new world coming into being".

It is one of several pieces by Hepworth in the auction.

articles.title: Guernsey named one of UK's best islands for travel
articles.summary: Guernsey finishes ahead of Jersey and behind only the Isles of Scilly in the Condé Nast awards.
articles.body:
Guernsey has been named the second-best island in the UK in the 2026 Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards, finishing ahead of Jersey and behind only the Isles of Scilly off Cornwall.

The island was ranked second in the magazine's list of the UK's top 10 islands, with Jersey placed fifth.

Visit Guernsey marketing manager Sam Claxton said the recognition reflected the mix of attractions visitors could enjoy on the island.

"Visitors really appreciate the unique combination that Guernsey offers," he said. "We've got beautiful beaches, we've got great cliff path. History as well. And then we've got this thriving food scene which has really started to grow."

He said visitors also regularly highlighted the island's welcoming atmosphere, adding: "I think it's the friendliness of our island that leaves the biggest impression."

The rankings were based on readers scoring destinations across several categories, including natural beauty, beaches, food, activities and value for money.

Claxton explained that Guernsey and Jersey had a "friendly rivalry", although the islands often worked together to promote the Channel Islands overseas, particularly in European markets.

He said awards such as these could help attract new visitors because they were based on independent recommendations from travellers.

"We do tend to see a bit of an uptick," he said.

"Recognition like this is incredibly valuable because, obviously, it helps put Guernsey in front of potential visitors who may not have considered us before."

Claxton said it was too early to know whether the latest ranking would boost visitor numbers, but suggested any increase was more likely to be seen next year.

articles.title: Yorkshire Wildlife Park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far
articles.summary: A recap on what we know about the attack which left a man dead at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
articles.body:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster remains closed after a man died in the tiger enclosure on Saturday.

Here's what we know so far about the attack.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was busy with visitors when the alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the park at about 13:30 BST to reports a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway.

Visitors were moved away from the area as the tiger attacked the man, who died a short time later.

The park confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

The park was closed on Saturday and has not yet reopened .

Yorkshire Wildlife Park spans 150 acres with 15 unique habitats featuring wide paths and raised viewing areas.

It focuses on large animal conservation, and counts species including lions, meerkats, lemurs, African penguins and sea lions among its residents.

The tigers are housed in the park's Land of the Tigers, which has a 300m-long raised walkway so visitors can watch the animals from above.

The park's website says people can witness the "majestic cats freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or playing in their very own waterfall pool".

The man has not been named, but eyewitnesses described seeing a man in his 20s on the walkway at the tiger enclosure, wearing headphones and "pacing around" minutes before the incident took place.

South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.

Speaking to the BBC, Ella Ford, 24, from Wirral, said she saw the same man had climbed up onto the barriers and was spoken to by a woman before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".

Ford said she then saw the man shouting for help and the tiger grabbed hold of him.

She estimates about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.

People nearby were confused, she said, and one man was "trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything".

Altai is a rare Amur tiger, also known as a Siberian tiger, the largest big cat in the world.

According to the park, the average weight for males is 160-190kg (25-30 stone), while females are smaller, at 110-130kg (17-20 stone).

Altai, now five years old, moved to Yorkshire Wildlife Park from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025.

The tiger was moved to Doncaster as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers, to join the park's resident tigress Tschuna.

Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."

A spokesperson for the park thanked everyone who showed concern after the incident.

In a statement on Sunday, they said: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the man who tragically lost his life.

"The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support.

"Many, many people have contacted us about Altai, the tiger.

"We can reassure everyone that he is safe and well and will not be euthanised as a result of this incident."

Dr David Sands, a human-companion animal practitioner at the Animal Behavioural Clinic in Chorley, Lancashire, said tigers were predators that would naturally attack.

"The animal is just being the animal that a million years of evolution has produced," he said.

"It is the top apex predator of its group of animals.

"I don't think any blame could be put on the animal itself."

He added: "Tigers are territorial. This is a male tiger and the incredible weight and power, there's only one outcome because the tiger is in captivity - the enclosure is its territory and a male who can be scented becomes either competition or prey.

"We're so used to seeing them on the small screen in wildlife documentaries.

"This is a very big animal that's got the power to bite and break through bones."

City of Doncaster Council confirmed a health and safety investigation had been launched into the death of the man in the enclosure.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.

"As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," he said.

"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident."

articles.title: Imran Khan’s stronghold in crisis: What's happening after emergency rule in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.summary: Pakistan’s political confrontation over jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has escalated after the federal government imposed emergency and
articles.body: Pakistan’s political confrontation over jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has escalated after the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending the authority of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial administration. The move, announced on Sunday, brings one of the party’s most important political strongholds under federal control and has intensified tensions between the government led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Khan’s supporters.President Asif Ali Zardari approved the measures under Articles 232(1) and 234(1) of Pakistan’s Constitution, citing a deteriorating security situation. Islamabad has accused the provincial government of failing to cooperate in the fight against terrorism, while the PTI has called the move an attempt to undermine its electoral mandate. A petition challenging the measures was filed in the Peshawar high court on Monday. Meanwhile, arrests, roadblocks, school closures and examination postponements have disrupted life in several districts as the authorities tighten security.Why governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?The federal government announced emergency and governor’s rule after a cabinet meeting on Sunday reviewed the security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan and has faced a persistent militant threat.In a statement, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s office said the cabinet had examined the deteriorating law and order situation and the provincial government’s “deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism”.Islamabad has accused the PTI-led administration of failing to take adequate action against militants and of not cooperating with federal authorities on security policy. Federal ministers have also alleged a “nexus” between the provincial government and terrorist groups, a charge the PTI disputes.Militants linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which shares an ideological affinity with the Afghan Taliban, have carried out attacks against security personnel and civilians in Pakistan. The federal government has argued that a coordinated response is necessary to counter the threat.The PTI, however, says it has been excluded from decisions concerning security in its own province. It has opposed military operations on its territory and called for a review of the counterterrorism strategy, including Islamabad’s approach to engagement with the Afghan Taliban.The disagreement contributed to the breakdown of talks between the federal government and PTI representatives on October 3.Under governor’s rule, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has taken charge of running the province. The federal government has also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power.The federal government has cited worsening law and order as the basis for its intervention. However, figures from the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), cited in the morning report, suggest the trend in reported deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was not identical to the national picture.Civilian and security personnel deaths in the province reportedly totalled 485 in the first nine months of 2026, a decline of 16 per cent from the same period in 2025. Across Pakistan, such deaths rose by 9 per cent over the corresponding period, according to the think-tank.The figures provide a counterpoint to the federal government’s account of the province’s security situation, but they do not, by themselves, establish whether the provincial administration adequately addressed militant activity or explain the reasons behind the change in fatalities.The new administration has pledged to strengthen the police and the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD), increase operational resources and continue intelligence-based operations against militants.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa apex committee vows continued operationsThe provincial Apex Committee held its first meeting under the new arrangement on Monday at the Governor House in Peshawar. It was co-chaired by Kundi and interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and attended by senior civil and military officials, including the Peshawar Corps Commander, chief secretary and inspector general of police.Kundi said tackling terrorism would be the administration’s immediate priority, pointing to what he described as a lack of coordination in counterterrorism efforts. “We can sacrifice our development, but never security,” he said, adding that the administration would “fulfil the demands of the Counter-Terrorism Department and police”, reported Dawn.He also promised a more results-oriented approach. “We have to show the difference,” Kundi said, adding that the administration would “work 24/7”.The governor highlighted the impact of militancy on daily life in districts such as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank and Waziristan, saying residents faced restrictions on their freedom to live and travel. He called for restoring normal movement and expressed hope that the new administration would be remembered for bringing peace to the province.Naqvi, meanwhile, accused the previous provincial government of failing to lead the fight against terrorism despite repeated requests from the Centre. “Today is the first time I can proudly say that the federal and the provincial governments are on the same page,” he said.Naqvi argued that security operations could not succeed without political leadership. “But any war, no matter how many resources you have, cannot be won until the government leads it,” he said.He cautioned that the situation would not change overnight but called on the governor, police, administration and federal government to work together.The committee resolved to continue intelligence-based operations and use all available resources to improve law and order. It also decided to strengthen the police and CTD with modern equipment, vehicles, armoured vehicles, weapons and additional personnel.Alongside security, the committee pledged to address public grievances, improve access to basic services and promote development in underdeveloped and conflict-affected areas.Imran Khan’s son condemns emergencyKasim Khan, son of the jailed former prime minister, condemned the emergency and governor’s rule, accusing Army Chief Asim Munir of using terrorism as a justification for another military operation in Pashtun areas.In a post on X, Kasim linked the measures to protests demanding his father’s release and alleged that the authorities were seeking to consolidate power through military action.“Pakistan belongs to its people, not its military,” he wrote.Kasim called for the restoration of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s democratic mandate and the immediate release of his father, detained family members, PTI representatives and other political prisoners. He also demanded that the right to protest be respected.The emergency was imposed as the PTI was holding a long march led by provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. The march called for Imran Khan’s release and access to medical treatment for him, while also opposing military operations that the party says have caused civilian deaths and damage.Afridi and seven other PTI leaders were taken into protective custody, according to reports. Afridi had vowed to continue the march before the provincial government’s powers were suspended, PTI reported.“There is no option other than accepting our demands,” Afridi said in a post on X before the takeover.“We will not back down,” he added. “Our long march will continue until the demands are met, in accordance with the law. Here, only Imran Khan’s policy will prevail.”The PTI has accused the federal government of using security concerns to weaken the party and undermine the elected provincial administration.“The arrest of chief minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the government’s actions,” PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram said in a statement.“These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” he alleged.The status of Junaid Akbar, a member of parliament and president of the PTI’s provincial chapter, requires separate confirmation before any arrest claim is treated as established.Petition challenges emergency and governor’s rule in courtThe federal government’s decision faced a legal challenge on Monday, with a petition filed in the Peshawar High Court less than 24 hours after the measures were introduced.Filed by Advocate Salman, the petition names President Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Governor Kundi as respondents. It argues that the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule is “unconstitutional, illegal and motivated by mala fide intentions”.The petitioner has also alleged that the measures violate fundamental rights and undermine the democratic mandate of the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Separately, opposition leaders met in Islamabad on Monday to discuss the emergency and its aftermath. Those present included PTI chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, National Assembly Opposition Leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai and PTI secretary general Barrister Salman Akram Raja. The participants also discussed challenging the measures in court.The legal challenge adds another front to the confrontation, with the province’s administrative status now under scrutiny alongside the government’s security justification.Roadblocks, arrests and school closuresThe impact of the emergency has varied across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with heightened security deployments, transport restrictions, school closures and arrests reported in several districts.In Peshawar, police remained deployed along major roads, while shipping containers blocked several routes, particularly around the cantonment area. Entry and exit points to Peshawar Cantt were closed, and access to areas including Khyber Road, parts of University Road and GT Road near Pir Zakori was restricted. Commuters were diverted to alternative routes.Traffic was relatively light on parts of the city’s road network on Monday afternoon. Educational institutions across the provincial capital remained closed. Internet and cellular services, which had been disrupted, were reported to have been fully restored in Peshawar, according to Dawn News.In Mardan, government and private schools, colleges and universities were shut, and examinations scheduled for the day were cancelled. Several education boards postponed secondary school examinations, including in Bannu, North Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan and Lakki Marwat. Fresh dates are to be announced.In Charsadda, police confirmed that 15 PTI workers had been arrested. In Shangla, more than two dozen party workers had been taken into custody, according to the district police chief. Authorities also imposed Section 144, prohibiting gatherings, and ordered intensified patrolling and checks at district entry and exit points.Containers were placed to block the Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway near Swabi, where internet and mobile services remained suspended. In Bannu, road restrictions were reported near the cantonment area.The situation was comparatively calm in parts of Khyber district. A PTI demonstration in Bara was dispersed by police, but roads, including the main Peshawar-Torkham Highway, remained open.In Lower South Waziristan, schools and colleges were closed, but markets and routine commercial activities continued. No major disruption to commercial activity or significant protests were reported there.Tank district imposed a one-month ban on pillion riding from October 10 to November 9 under Section 144, citing security concerns.The differing conditions across districts underline the uneven impact of the emergency. While restrictions have affected transport, education and political activity in several areas, routine life has continued in others.Why Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is important to Imran Khan’s PTIKhyber Pakhtunkhwa has been a key political base for Imran Khan’s PTI, which has governed the province since 2013. The party remained a major force in the 2024 elections despite Khan’s imprisonment and the difficulties faced by its candidates.Khan, a former Pakistan cricket captain who served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022, was removed from office through a parliamentary no-confidence vote. He has been in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi since 2023 and faces more than 100 cases, including corruption and charges related to inciting violence.Candidates backed by Khan won the largest number of seats in the National Assembly in the 2024 elections, but the party was kept out of federal power as other political parties formed the government.The takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa therefore carries significance beyond the change in provincial administration. It places a crucial PTI-governed province under a federal arrangement at a time when the party is mobilising supporters for Khan’s release and challenging Islamabad’s counterterrorism policy.The PTI maintains that the federal government’s actions undermine the provincial electorate’s mandate. Islamabad, in turn, argues that the security situation requires decisive intervention and closer coordination between the provincial and federal authorities.What nowThe imposition of governor’s rule has sharpened the divide between the PML-N-led federal government and the PTI, which has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for more than a decade. Their dispute centres on responsibility for worsening militancy, the scope of military operations and the provincial administration’s role in security policymaking.The Centre maintains that the provincial government failed to adequately support counterterrorism efforts. The PTI says it was excluded from decisions concerning its own province and argues that the takeover undermines the democratic mandate of its voters.With the emergency facing a legal challenge, PTI leaders in custody and security restrictions disrupting parts of the province, the confrontation is now unfolding on political, judicial and security fronts. The federal government has pledged a more coordinated campaign against terrorism, while the opposition is demanding the restoration of the province’s elected administration.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Himalayas are getting a new war machine as Indian Army expands its drone arsenal
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Indian Army has placed an order for 225 First-Person View (FPV) drones that will be deployed in the high-altitude environs of Ladakh.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Army has placed an order for 225 First-Person View (FPV) drones that will be deployed in the high-altitude environs of Ladakh.The remote and desolate region has several high-altitude posts, some of which are located on ridges that rise above 18,000 feet. The Army has increased its deployment in the area since the Galwan clashes in 2020 and the stand-off that followed. China has also been demonstrating and operating drones in the region since then.China has since set up a drone centre near Mount Everest, with the aim of advancing drone technology for border patrols, security, logistics and emergency operations.Another significant development is that a Chinese-origin drone has reportedly reached an altitude above Mount Everest, while a Nepali firm has been using Chinese drones for logistics in the same region, including on the world's highest mountain itself.Tested at 17,500 feet: The Army's new drone orderGurgaon-based Aerodrone Robotics Pvt Ltd, founded by retired Army officer Lt Col Randeep Hundal, will deliver these FPV drones to the Army. The firm won the contract following a lengthy competitive evaluation and field trials that included flights at altitudes of up to 17,500 feet.The drones were assessed on endurance, accuracy, speed and other functional requirements, including performance in the thin, cold air where much of the Army's frontier work is carried out.The order comes as the force is in the middle of a wide-ranging modernisation drive, with unmanned systems becoming one of its central priorities. The contract's value has not been disclosed, and the number of drones is modest by the standards of the Army's recent procurement plans.Reports on the order note that 17,500 feet was the altitude reached during the trials and should not be read as the drones' certified operational ceiling.What stands out is how the systems were tested. The Army has been trialling drones from Indian manufacturers in the high-altitude terrain of Ladakh and Spiti in Himachal Pradesh, where difficult terrain and extreme weather place heavy demands on equipment.The process also has a history. Two years ago, the Army held the second Him-Drone-a-Thon at Wari La in Ladakh, at over 15,000 feet, where more than 20 manufacturers showcased surveillance, logistics, loitering munition, swarm and FPV systems designed for high altitudes.Seen against that backdrop, the 225-drone order marks a step from demonstrations to an actual contract.Why drones are changing the way wars are foughtOur drones have taken off from 16,000 feet and climbed beyond 18,000 feet, operating in some of the world's most challenging terrain. Light enough for a soldier to carry, they give him the decisive advantage of spotting threats before being detected.In modern warfare, whoever sees first, strikes first. These indigenous drones will transform how the Indian Army patrols, dominates terrain and engages the enemy. Our mission is to give every soldier that technological edge.The reason the Army is investing so much in drones lies in how wars are now being fought. In Ukraine, what began as a contest involving tanks and artillery has increasingly become a drone war, with drones estimated to account for about 70% of Russian casualties, according to recent Ukrainian media reports.Drones have also been central to recent fighting involving Israel. Their uses now range from surveillance and logistics to precision strikes and communications, allowing forces to strike targets or monitor a frontline without directly exposing soldiers and pilots to the same risks.For a small, inexpensive aircraft, that is a remarkable return, and it is one reason armies around the world are rethinking their concepts of operations around these machines.For India, the case is especially strong along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China and the Line of Control (LoC) with Pakistan, where troops operate at altitudes as high as 21,000 feet overlooking the Siachen Glacier.These conditions degrade both human performance and conventional equipment. Supplying remote forward posts has traditionally depended on soldiers, mules and an ageing fleet of Cheetah helicopters.Helicopter sorties are costly and weather-dependent. Drones could offer a faster, cheaper and safer alternative for some tasks.Facing the digitised air defence and surveillance networks that China has built along the LAC also calls for a modern, agile and unmanned response.Thin air, freezing batteries: Why flying drones in the Himalayas is difficultThe terrain makes this a difficult engineering problem. At 15,000 feet, atmospheric density is roughly 40% lower than at sea level. The thinner air leaves propellers with less air to work with, reducing lift and thrust.Motors, which rely on airflow for cooling, can run hotter and burn out under heavy loads. Operators may therefore need larger or higher-pitch propellers or different motor configurations, which can increase power consumption.Cold compounds the problem, as lithium-based batteries perform less efficiently in freezing temperatures, causing voltage sag and a reduction in usable capacity. Depending on the conditions, battery capacity can fall significantly, sometimes to around half its normal level.Batteries may need to be preheated before launch and insulated during flight. Jagged peaks and ridges can also block radio signals, causing sudden video or control blackouts, while stray radio interference can affect sensitive FPV receivers.The Indian companies building the Army's drone fleetAerodrone works in the military unmanned aerial systems segment and has developed combat, surveillance and logistics platforms, along with operator training and technical support.It describes its platforms as military-hardened, with software developed in-house, an approach meant to provide greater control over configuration and allow systems to be adapted to specific operational needs.That fits the government's push for Atmanirbharta in defence, where owning the software matters as much as building the airframe.Aerodrone is not the only supplier, though. A study by the Centre for Joint Warfare Studies earlier this year lists several other Indian FPV drone manufacturers whose systems have already been inducted or are undergoing trials.Inducted platforms include those from Apollyon Dynamics, Quantum Tech, which offers standard and fibre-optic variants, DroneYards and Rising Star, while Optiemus and others were at the trial stage.The same study puts one inducted vendor's airframe at about Rs 1.4 lakh. That is a single vendor's price and not the cost of this order, but it gives a sense of how inexpensive these systems can be compared with a helicopter sortie.The picture is of an Army buying relatively small numbers of drones as it develops its concepts of operations.From Operation Sindoor to new drone units: The Army's modernisation pushThe order is one part of a much larger overhaul. General Upendra Dwivedi, who retired as Army chief in June 2026, described the present period as the force's 'Decade of Transformation', with changes cutting across its structure, equipment and training.New formations are being introduced, including Rudra all-arms brigades, Shaktibaan regiments, Divyastra batteries and Bhairav battalions. Drones sit at the centre of this effort rather than at its edge.Current Army chief General Dhiraj Seth has also stressed modernisation through his 'VIJAY' mantra, in which 'I' stands for innovation and transformation, while 'A' stands for Atmanirbharta.These initiatives show how the Army sees the road ahead.A significant push came after the active phase of Operation Sindoor, following which the Army carried out a comprehensive review with a sharper focus on unmanned systems, counter-drone capabilities, electronic warfare and faster procurement.The Army has decided to place an Ashni drone platoon in every infantry battalion. These platoons operate drones that can be used for both surveillance and strike missions.The Ministry of Defence's Annual Report for 2025-26 adds that the Army has built in-house drone manufacturing capacity with the help of small firms.Training is the other half of the effort. The Army wants every soldier to learn to operate a drone, just as soldiers are trained to use weapons.The Army has also raised a dedicated Baaz battalion to manage the induction, upgrading and replenishment of remotely piloted aircraft.The next challengeElectronic warfare is emerging as another important aspect of drone warfare, as radio-controlled FPV drones are vulnerable to jamming, a lesson highlighted by the war in Ukraine.A Centre for Joint Warfare Studies (CENJOWS) study argues that new FPV purchases should favour fibre-optic variants.Apart from this, the armed forces are also looking at kinetic methods, such as guns and low-cost missiles, to bring down drones, as well as using drone swarms. The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has also developed laser-based systems to bring down drones.As India works to develop both drones and counter-drone systems, many of these platforms could be deployed along the ridgelines overlooking the Tibetan plateau, often referred to as the Roof of the World.Their deployment could ease the burden on soldiers and equipment alike.As combat increasingly incorporates autonomous and remotely operated systems, these technologies are expected to reach even India's most remote frontiers.The procurement of these platforms will not only give Indian soldiers improved surveillance and strike capabilities but also strengthen the domestic defence industry and expand the country's technological capabilities.

articles.title: UK universities withdraw admission offers to Indian, Pakistani, Nigerian students as visa refusals rise
articles.summary: Universities in the United Kingdom are withdrawing admission offers to international students, including those from India, Pakistan, Nigeria and
articles.body: Universities in the United Kingdom are withdrawing admission offers to international students, including those from India, Pakistan, Nigeria and Bangladesh, fearing that the UK government's visa crackdown will result in a blanket ban on recruiting international students, the Financial Times reported.In a new rule since June 1, institutions have been required to keep visa refusals rate below 5% -- down from 10%. Universities that repeatedly fail to meet the thresholds can face enforcement action and then lose their student sponsor licence.Basically, the UK government wants universities to have fewer student visa refusals. Some universities, worried about breaching the new threshold, are responding by withdrawing admission offers from applicants they think might be refused visas.International students are only able to apply for a study visa after receiving an offer from a university, meaning the visa application is withdrawn if the offer is later revoked. While visa applications can be withdrawn for other reasons, universities said the main driver had been an increase in their revoking offers.According to a Financial Times analysis of UK Home Office data, 10.5% of UK study visa applications were withdrawn in the first half of 2026, compared with 2.3% during the same period in 2025 and 0.4% in 2023. Universities have told the newspaper that withdrawing admission offers pre-emptively has been a major reason for the increase.Pakistan recorded the highest proportion of withdrawn applications among the nationalities highlighted in the analysis, at 40.9% in January-June 2026, compared with 3% in the corresponding period last year. Around 15 universities are thought to have suspended recruitment from Pakistan entirely this year.Bangladesh's rate rose from 7.1% to 23.5%, while Nigeria's increased from 4.5% to 22.7%.For Indian applicants, the proportion of withdrawn study visa applications increased from 1.2% in the first half of 2025 to 5.2% in the first half of 2026.These figures refer to withdrawn applications, not visa refusals, the FT clarified.Universities raise concerns over student visa refusalsSir David Bell, vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, told the FT that the unexpected rise in refusals had prompted universities to take pre-emptive action, including reducing recruitment from markets facing greater scrutiny.Professor Steven McGuire, deputy vice-chancellor of the University of East Anglia, told the FT that the university began withdrawing offers from applicants in certain countries towards the end of 2025 after refusals increased significantly.The UK government, however, maintains that tighter oversight is necessary to prevent abuse of the immigration system. Migration and Citizenship Minister Mike Tapp has said the country will continue to welcome genuine international students but that the student visa route must not be used as a means of accessing asylum or illegal employment.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, YouTube star and real estate investor Kris Krohn commissioned a Utah estate; the 28,446-sq-ft compound is now listed for $13.95 million, featuring a hydraulic indoor pool that transforms into a column-free ballroom
articles.summary: YouTube star and real estate investor Kris Krohn has put his Utah mansion up for sale.
articles.body: YouTube star and real estate investor Kris Krohn has put his Utah mansion up for sale. The 28,446-sq-ft estate, commissioned in 2017, is listed for $13.95 million. The listing is handled by Paul Benson of Engel & Völkers Park City.According to the listing, this residence has a feature that has “almost no parallel in North America”. The mansion has an indoor pool built on a hydraulic floor system inspired by The O Theater at the Bellagio. “On command, the pool descends, and the floor rises to form a column-free ballroom, ready for seated dinners, performances, productions, or private events at full scale,” the listing says.Inside the Utah mansionThe estate spans 1.64 acres and has two connected wings. The family wing, measuring 8,500 sq ft, serves as the daily residence. It has five bedrooms, a private office, a chef’s kitchen, a caretaker’s apartment, and a great room framed by double-height glass walls that capture the breathtaking views of the Wasatch Range.The newer wing is where the scale becomes apparent. It has the pool and ballroom, a commercial-grade gym with a sparring ring for boxing and MMA, and a racquetball court. A spa also features a dry sauna, a steam room, a cold plunge, a float room, and a massage suite. The wing also has an executive office with its own conference room and a second kitchen that opens straight into the ballroom.A dedicated space for carsAnother highlight of the mansion is its carefully designed garage. It is a motorhead’s dream. The garage space measures more than 5,500 sq ft. “Most of it is a gallery for a car collection, with elevated display platforms and a lounge where friends can gather after a weekend drive. A 1,000-sq-ft RV garage with a 12-foot door keeps the motorhome or boat packed and ready for the next Lake Powell trip, and the family wing has its own three-car garage for everyday driving,” the listing says.A separate RV garage accommodates a motorhome or boat, and the agent points to Lake Powell as the natural destination for the latter. According to the listing, it is “a visionary estate, built without compromise, for the buyer who recognises what it is”. The massive compound overlooks the valley, with breathtaking views of the Wasatch Range, Utah Lake, and Loafer Mountain. “What impresses me most is that it still feels like a home. The family wing is separate, with its own kitchen, a great room with a two-storey wall of glass, and a hot tub on the deck above the valley. You can host a big event on Saturday night and wake up to a quiet house on Sunday morning,” the listing agent said.Benson does not expect a holiday-home buyer. “Much of what our team sells in Park City is a second home, and this is the opposite. Nothing here is set up for a few weeks a year. You work here, train here, and host here every day. Utah County is also where people live full-time and build their companies, so I expect the buyer to make this their main home. The one exception I can see is a buyer from out of state who wants a base in Utah that is big enough to bring everyone together several times a year,” he told the outlet. He also has an ideal buyer in mind: “Someone who has built a business and wants everything in one place.”“My guess is an entrepreneur or founder who already lives in Utah, most likely with a company in Utah County or Silicon Slopes, who works from home, trains every day, collects cars, and loves to host,” he added.Such a person would normally need an office, a gym, an event venue, and a separate building for the cars. This estate has all of them. “Either way, it will be someone who likes to bring people together, because that is what this home was built for.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Ted Turner brought an environmental cartoon to TV in 1990; the foundation it inspired now backs young conservationists in 11 countries
articles.summary: When Ted Turner died on 6 May 2026, aged 87, tributes focused largely on the media empire he built and his role in founding CNN.
articles.body: When Ted Turner died on 6 May 2026, aged 87, tributes focused largely on the media empire he built and his role in founding CNN. Another part of his legacy began with an environmental cartoon. Turner and his colleague Barbara Pyle developed the idea for Captain Planet and the Planeteers in the late 1980s, before the animated series launched in 1990. It followed young heroes who joined forces to confront environmental threats, introducing ecological issues to a younger audience through entertainment. In 1991, Turner and Pyle co-founded the Captain Planet Foundation, which continues to support environmental projects and help young people develop solutions in their communities. Its programmes include school gardens, environmental science challenges and youth-led conservation campaigns.Captain Planet and the Planeteers: how Ted Turner and Barbara Pyle brought environmental issues to televisionTurner’s environmental interests extended well beyond television. According to the Ted Turner Legacy page published by Turner Enterprises, he established the Turner Foundation in 1990, a family foundation focused on environmental protection, habitat conservation, sustainable living and community well-being. That same year, Captain Planet and the Planeteers launched on television. Created by Turner and Pyle, the animated series aired from 1990 to 1996. The show followed five young Planeteers from different parts of the world who combined their elemental powers to summon Captain Planet and confront threats such as pollution, poaching and deforestation. Its premise placed environmental protection at the centre of the story, presenting ecological problems in a format designed to engage younger viewers. The Captain Planet Foundation’s history explains how the series became the inspiration for its work with young people.The cartoon was one part of a broader conservation record. In 1997, Turner pledged $1 billion to support the United Nations, a commitment that led to the establishment of the United Nations Foundation in 1998. He also established the Turner Endangered Species Fund in 1997 to support biodiversity conservation, including work involving threatened species. Turner Enterprises says that, at the time of his death, Turner’s holdings included approximately 2 million acres of land and a herd of 45,000 bison. He also created the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture to help protect his landholdings and advance research and education related to conservation and agriculture. Turner’s philanthropy extended beyond environmental conservation. TIME named him its Man of the Year in 1991, and he signed the Giving Pledge, committing to give the majority of his wealth to charitable causes. His conservation work reflected a long-standing interest in protecting natural systems, while the cartoon offered a way to bring environmental issues to a global television audience.Captain Planet Foundation origins: how a cartoon’s merchandising revenue supported youth projectsThe Captain Planet Foundation was co-founded by Turner and Pyle in 1991 as a corporate foundation within Turner Broadcasting System. According to its official history, Pyle negotiated for a portion of the cartoon’s merchandising revenue to support young people working to solve environmental problems. The idea was to turn the show’s message into practical opportunities for children and young people to act on environmental concerns beyond the television screen. In the early 2000s, the foundation separated from Turner Broadcasting System and became an independent 501(c)(3) public charity. The foundation’s profiles give 2002 as the year of the transition. The transition was organised by Turner’s daughter Laura Turner Seydel and her husband, Rutherford. Seydel went on to chair the foundation and remains associated with its work.Over time, the organisation expanded beyond its original grant-making model into programmes combining environmental education with practical projects. Its work now includes school gardens, hands-on science challenges and youth-led environmental campaigns. These initiatives aim to help young people identify problems in their communities and develop solutions, rather than limiting environmental education to classroom lessons. The foundation also broadened its focus to ocean conservation. In 2018, it partnered with Lonely Whale to launch Ocean Heroes Bootcamp, which trained young activists to develop campaigns against plastic pollution. The foundation has reported that more than 1,200 young activists from 56 countries were trained within three years. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Project Giving Gardens used school and community gardening networks to support food access. The foundation reported that more than 100,000 pounds of produce were harvested and distributed in 2020, equivalent to approximately 400,000 servings.Captain Planet Foundation programmes today: school gardens, STEM challenges and youth-led climate actionThe foundation’s current programmes continue to connect environmental learning with practical projects. Its official website identifies Project Learning Garden, the Green Heart STEM Challenge and Planeteer Alliance as key parts of its work. Project Learning Garden helps elementary schools establish and maintain gardens for hands-on learning. The foundation’s 2025 annual report lists programme locations across 41 US states. The Green Heart STEM Challenge serves middle-school students, inviting them to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions. In 2025, more than 1,000 students in the Atlanta and Houston metropolitan areas took part in challenges addressing issues including electronic waste, food waste, fast fashion and single-use plastics. The foundation says three winning teams received mentorship and implementation grants to develop their ideas.Planeteer Alliance extends the model to young people beyond the classroom. Open to people aged 10 to 25, the programme provides environmental leadership training, campaign-design resources and opportunities to collaborate with other young advocates. Its 2025 annual report says participants recruited and trained more than 2,500 peers during the year. The report’s overview also records 22 youth-led WIND Summits and more than 60 other action-related events across 11 countries. These figures describe reported programme activity in 2025, rather than cumulative reach. The report describes several projects supported through the alliance. In Farato, The Gambia, Sanna Jambang and his team created a clean-energy demonstration site where residents could see solar energy in action, ask questions and explore how it might be used in their own homes. Elsewhere, projects have addressed reforestation, waste management, sustainable transport and conservation education. The foundation also highlights Daniel Olajuyigbe’s work with a team organising beach clean-ups in Lagos, Nigeria. The example illustrates how young participants have applied environmental campaigning to local waste problems. These examples are reported by the organisation and illustrate the range of activities it supports, rather than independently measured evidence of long-term environmental impact.Following Turner’s death, the Captain Planet Foundation said it would continue as his living legacy. More than three decades after the cartoon first aired, its work remains centred on a similar idea: environmental education can extend beyond awareness and encourage young people to take part in solving problems where they live. Through gardens, science challenges and youth-led campaigns, the foundation continues to put that idea into practice.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Laiba Ijaz suicide: Pakistan gold medalist commits suicide after visa scam; suspect on 5-day remand
articles.summary: A 20-year-old Pakistani student, Laiba Ijaz, died by suicide on October 9 after allegedly being defrauded of millions of rupees by an agent who promised
articles.body: A 20-year-old Pakistani student, Laiba Ijaz, died by suicide on October 9 after allegedly being defrauded of millions of rupees by an agent who promised to secure her admission to Harvard University, a scholarship and a US visa. An Islamabad court on Monday granted police five days of physical remand of the main accused, Muhammad Noman, in connection with the case, Voice PK reported.Judicial magistrate Zunaira Zafar passed the order after police produced Noman in court with his face covered. Police had sought 10 days of remand to investigate his alleged role, verify evidence and examine witness statements.Pakistan's Senate Standing Committee on Human Rights has also sought a detailed inquiry into Laiba's death and the alleged fraud. According to police reporting, the committee will meet on October 15. Islamabad's inspector general of police, the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) director general and the Higher Education Commission chairman have been directed to attend.The committee has sought details of the case registration, the suspect's arrest and the investigation so far. It has also asked authorities to report on steps taken to cancel the licence of the educational consultant accused of issuing fake documents.Family alleges loss of Pakistani Rs 9.3 millionAccording to local reports, Laiba was found hanging from a tree in Islamabad's Sector G-10 on Friday, October 9. Police said she had paid an agent Rs 5 million to arrange her travel to the United States but was later given fake documents.Laiba had left home around 2pm, telling her mother she would return shortly. When she failed to come back, her family searched for her and tracked her location using her mobile phone. They found her body and informed the police, who took it to a hospital.The Media Line reported that Laiba was a physics gold medallist and scholarship holder who aspired to become a scientist and study at Harvard. Her family allegedly lost Rs 9.3 million, approximately $34,000, to those promising her admission, a scholarship and a US visa.Her father had sold milk and yoghurt on Islamabad's streets since 1994 to support his family's education. To finance Laiba's studies abroad, he reportedly sold land intended for the family's home, while her mother pawned her jewellery. Laiba had also declined a scholarship in Saudi Arabia because she wanted to pursue her ambitions in the United States.Shortly before her death, Laiba called her brother-in-law and said, "Don't tell my father about the fraud committed against me; otherwise, he will die."Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an investigation into the case.What FIR allegesAccording to the police FIR, Laiba's father said the family had met Noman around six to seven months before her death. Noman allegedly introduced himself as a senior official in Islamabad and offered to arrange a US study visa for Laiba for Rs 9.3 million.The father alleged that he paid Rs 2.1 million in cash to Noman at G-10 Markaz in the presence of witnesses. Laiba transferred another Rs 2.9 million through her mobile and bank accounts, according to the complaint.Noman allegedly supplied documents that later turned out to be fake. He also reportedly presented a forged receipt showing a transfer of $20,000 into Laiba's bank account to help prepare a bank statement. The father said Noman stopped answering his calls after the family questioned him about the documents.The father also accused a woman identified as Fatima Sarwar, alias Aiza, of involvement in the alleged fraud. She reportedly contacted Laiba and demanded more money. He said Laiba had been in severe distress for five to six days before her death and blamed Noman and Aiza for her suffering.A separate complaint lodged by Laiba's uncle, Amjad Rehman, with the FIA's Anti-Human Trafficking Circle named Noman and Aiza as accused in an alleged conspiracy to defraud the family of Rs 9.3 million. The complaint alleged that Rs 2.9 million was transferred to Noman's bank account, while the remaining amount was paid in cash at a shop in Gulistan Plaza, G-10 Markaz.Senior lawyer Raja Naveed Kiyani said police and the FIA could register separate FIRs over the same incident. He explained that the FIA could pursue its own investigation and seek Noman's custody through the court after he was transferred from police custody to judicial remand.The allegations against Noman and Aiza are yet to be established in court. The case has also highlighted concerns over fraudulent educational consultants who target Pakistani students seeking admission and scholarships abroad.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
